diagnosis.title: Verification policy overgeneralization
diagnosis.summary: A standing checking policy applies beyond the risks or decisions it was meant to address, producing redundant verification even when the agent follows its instructions.

intervention-ref.when: A specific editable instruction or workflow triggers checks without a relevant changed state, unresolved question, or still-unmet acceptance need.

predictions.p: After narrowing that rule, verification overrun should decline for the affected class of work while required checks and defect detection remain intact. The reduction should occur at the rule's trigger points, not uniformly across unrelated tasks.

Continued extra checks after the revised rule reaches the agent favor another cause. Fewer checks with more missed defects suggest the scope was narrowed too far; slower delivery from another bottleneck may remain.

definition.p: A verification policy should connect each required check to a decision, risk, or acceptance condition and define when enough evidence has been gathered. A broad or self-retriggering rule instead demands another check irrespective of whether the relevant state changed or the question was already answered.
The agent may be complying perfectly with that rule. The proposed pathology is in the configured checking policy, not an inference about caution, anxiety, or intent.

criterion.title: An operative rule triggers the work
criterion.p: Identify the actual instruction or workflow rule and the decision points where it caused the extra checks. Similar wording in an unused file is insufficient.

criterion.title: The trigger exceeds the checking need
criterion.p: Establish that the rule covers a class of work whose relevant verification need is already satisfied or absent. Name the missing justification; elapsed time or passing results alone do not establish waste.

criterion.title: The policy produces excess checking
criterion.p: Following the rule produces excessive verification, with delay or resource use traceable to the extra checks. Equivalent rereads may also match repeated retrieval.

exclusion.p: The checks address an unmet acceptance condition, relevant risk, new change, or an agreed repeatability study.
The chosen check is appropriate but expensive because of its implementation or environment. Slow execution alone does not establish an overgeneral policy.

alternative.title: The system loses evidence that checking finished

discriminator.p: Inspect whether the prior result reaches the later turn. Repetition after a transition may instead reflect context handoff loss.
Compare code, environment, and failures at each trigger. The later check may answer a genuinely new question.

alternative.title: Extra checking is not prescribed by the rule

discriminator.p: Compare the instruction with the chosen action. If the rule already limits scope and the agent exceeds it, this policy explanation is incomplete.

investigation.p: Map extra checks to the rule and the question each result could answer. Include a healthy task where the same rule is useful. Inspect ordinary future work after a scoped policy change; a costly replay study is not a prerequisite.

interventions.p: Give verification a scope and stopping condition changes the offending policy. The maintainer must have authority to change it; an executing agent should not silently bypass a mandatory gate.

evidence-and-uncertainty.p: This is an unvalidated working model. An inefficient-looking check does not by itself establish a bad rule, and the entry provides no measured effect of changing one. Agreement about justified verification may vary with task risk.
